claims.text: Calling `toString` on an `Output<T>` without proper handling is not supported and can produce placeholder text like `Calling [toString] on an [Output<T>] is not supported` in a log line, a generated file, or a resource property.

The Pulumi documentation page at /docs/iac/operations/troubleshooting/output-values/ contains a rundown of symptoms of treating an output as if it were already a plain value, including the placeholder text `Calling [toString] on an [Output<T>] is not supported`.
Creating resources inside an `apply` call should be avoided whenever possible.
Resources created inside an `apply` call will not appear in `pulumi preview` unless the output's value is already known.
Because resources created inside `apply` will not appear in `pulumi preview` unless the output's value is already known, the preview output may not match the actual changes when `pulumi up` is run.

Pulumi resource properties are represented as Outputs rather than plain values because their real values are not known until the resource providing them has actually been created or updated.
Pulumi's Output representation of resource properties is central to how Pulumi builds a dependency graph and runs `pulumi preview`.
If you concatenate, log, or otherwise convert a Pulumi output value to a string directly instead of going through `apply` or an equivalent helper, Pulumi does not raise an error by default.
When a Pulumi output value is converted to a string directly instead of through `apply`, Pulumi silently substitutes a placeholder message in place of the value.
In TypeScript, calling `console.log` with a template string that embeds an Output property (e.g. `${bucket.bucketName}`) silently produces a broken string and does not throw an exception.

In Pulumi's TypeScript SDK, calling `toString` on an Output produces a string containing the literal text "Calling [toString] on an [Output<T>] is not supported", followed by guidance to use `apply` or `pulumi.interpolate` instead.

In Pulumi's TypeScript SDK, calling `JSON.stringify()` on an Output, or letting an Output flow into a JSON body, produces a string "Calling [toJSON] on an [Output<T>] is not supported" rather than the value.
In Python, formatting an output value into an f-string (e.g. `f"The bucket name is {bucket.bucket}"`) produces a broken string and logs a warning, without raising an exception.
In Pulumi's Python SDK, calling `__str__` on an Output produces a string containing the literal text "Calling __str__ on an Output[T] is not supported", and Pulumi also logs a warning.
In Pulumi's Python SDK, passing an Output to `json.dumps()` fails outright with `TypeError: Object of type Output is not JSON serializable`.
Pulumi's Python SDK provides `Output.json_dumps()` as the supported alternative to calling `json.dumps()` directly on an Output.
In Pulumi's Go SDK, passing a `pulumi.StringOutput` where a `string` is expected is a compile error rather than a runtime surprise.
In Pulumi's Go SDK, the fix for output-to-string conversion errors is to resolve the value inside `ApplyT` and pass the result on, rather than reading a `pulumi.StringOutput` as a plain `string`.

In C#, calling `Console.WriteLine` with a string interpolation that embeds an Output property (e.g. `$"The bucket name is {bucket.BucketName}"`) silently produces a broken string and does not throw an exception.

In Pulumi's C# SDK, calling `ToString` on an Output produces a string containing the literal text "Calling [ToString] on an [Output<T>] is not supported", followed by guidance to use `Apply` or `Output.Format` instead.

Because the output-to-string mistake fails by producing a string rather than throwing, the mistake is easy to miss during development since the program runs and `pulumi up` succeeds before the placeholder text surfaces later.

Setting the environment variable `PULUMI_ERROR_OUTPUT_STRING=true` in Pulumi programs written in TypeScript, Python, or C# causes the code that would otherwise produce the placeholder text to throw an exception at the point of the mistake instead.
Pulumi's TypeScript SDK provides `pulumi.interpolate` and `pulumi.concat` as string-composition helpers for working with Outputs.
Pulumi's Python SDK provides `Output.concat`, `Output.format`, and `Output.json_dumps` as string-composition helpers for working with Outputs.
Pulumi's Go SDK provides `pulumi.Sprintf` and `pulumi.JSONMarshal` as string-composition helpers for working with Outputs.
Pulumi's C# SDK provides `Output.Format` as a string-composition helper for working with Outputs.
A value read out of a Pulumi output inside an `apply`/`Apply` callback is only available inside that callback or in another output derived from it.

Assigning a value read inside an `apply` callback to an outer variable and using that variable later outside the callback does not work as expected, because the variable is still undefined when read outside the callback.
The `apply` callback in Pulumi runs asynchronously once the output resolves, which in general is after the rest of the program's top-level code has already finished running.

The timing issue where an outer variable is undefined after an `apply` callback is not a timing bug fixable by adding a delay, because the callback runs when the Pulumi engine resolves the dependency graph, not on the program's clock.
Most Pulumi resource inputs accept outputs as well as plain values.
A resource's logical name is a position that cannot accept a Pulumi output value directly.

In a dynamically typed Pulumi SDK language, an `if` statement evaluated directly on an output object is generally always true regardless of what the output resolves to, because the output object itself is a true value in a boolean context.
In a statically typed Pulumi SDK language, branching directly on an output (e.g. `Output<bool>`) is usually a compile error because an `Output<bool>` is not a `bool`.

A value that is already known when a Pulumi program starts, such as a stack configuration setting read with `pulumi.Config`, an environment variable, or a hardcoded flag, is a plain value that branches exactly as expected.
In Pulumi's TypeScript SDK, writing `if (vpc.vpcId) { ... }` does not work as intended because the branch is evaluated on the Output object rather than its resolved value.
In Pulumi's TypeScript SDK, deriving a new Output via `vpc.vpcId.apply((id) => (id.startsWith("vpc-0") ? 3 : 6))` correctly produces an Output whose value depends on the branch condition.
A resource's logical name (the first argument to its constructor) must be a known plain value while the Pulumi program is still being evaluated, before any resource actually exists.
Loop bounds and map keys used while authoring a Pulumi program must be known plain values while the program is still being evaluated, before any resource actually exists.
Passing a Pulumi output as a resource's logical name, loop bound, or map key fails to compile in TypeScript, Go, and C#, because these positions are typed as plain strings or numbers in those SDKs.
Python's dynamic typing does not catch at compile time the error of passing a Pulumi output as a resource name, loop bound, or map key.
In Pulumi's Python SDK, passing an output as a resource's logical name raises `TypeError: Expected resource name to be a string` at runtime.
In Pulumi's Python SDK, using an output as a loop bound via `range(some_output)` raises `TypeError: 'Output' object cannot be interpreted as an integer`.

In Pulumi's Python SDK, using an output as a dictionary key does not raise an error, but instead falls back to comparing and hashing the output object itself, silently keying the lookup on the wrong thing.

Pulumi supports restructuring dependent resources into a later, separate stack that consumes an earlier stack's outputs through a StackReference, when data cannot be known until an earlier resource has been provisioned.
Trying to `await` a Pulumi output or read its value synchronously either doesn't compile, fails at runtime, or quietly returns placeholder text instead of the value.
Pulumi has no supported way to block a program and pull a resolved value out of an output synchronously.
The Pulumi CLI command `pulumi stack output <name>` reads a single stack output after a deployment.
A Pulumi `StackReference` from another Pulumi program can be used to consume one stack's outputs as another stack's inputs.
The Pulumi Automation API exposes an `outputs` field on the result of running an update, for example `res.Outputs` in Go, for programmatically driving deployments.
